Portable Agent Governance at Solo-Developer Scale: A Four-Domain Case Study

Summary

This is about a file-based execution protocol, maintained by hand across four independent, real production projects (a crypto trading system, an e-commerce web app, an AI decision system, and an agent infrastructure layer). The person who built it doesn't write a single line of code. They design the architecture, set the rule hierarchy, and enforce the discipline; an AI writes and technically executes the code. That split isn't presented here as a caveat — it's what the system actually is: not a code project, but a decision-making and oversight protocol. Its quality can be judged independently of whether its designer writes code.

Enterprise AI agent governance (MI9, Microsoft Agent 365, JFrog AI Catalog) offers systems optimized for scale and automation: centralized telemetry, policy-as-code, runtime enforcement. But even their own literature admits two things: (1) coverage varies by framework, and (2) setup and maintenance cost is disproportionate for solo or small-scale use.

The protocol family described here (CORE.md / AGENT.md / SESSION_INDEX.md and their derivatives) runs on a different assumption: not a static template, but a system that revises itself over time. A concrete failure in one project gets written into the file as a dated, justified rule — and that rule gets inherited by a completely different project in a different domain.

1. The limits enterprise governance admits to itself

Enterprise investment in agentic AI governance is growing fast — according to IDC, organizations now allocate an average of 16.7% of total planned AI spending to AI/agent security and governance. But the same sources show implementation lagging far behind intent:

  • Only 13% believe they have adequate AI governance, despite 76% having a Chief AI Officer.
  • Among 235 large-enterprise security leaders, 92% lack full visibility into their AI identities; 82% discovered AI agents on their networks they didn't know existed.
  • More than 40% of agentic AI projects are expected to be cancelled by 2027 due to inadequate controls.

Academic/enterprise runtime governance frameworks like MI9 implicitly admit the same thing. MI9's own paper states: "Coverage depends on the instrumentation capabilities of each framework: callback-enabled frameworks support comprehensive behavioral monitoring, while API-wrapper architectures primarily expose action events." In other words, the design goal is framework-agnostic, but real-world coverage isn't.

Bottom line: enterprise governance is necessary at large scale, but at small-to-mid scale it's both heavy and incomplete.

2. An alternative model: a living protocol under a single decision-maker

Four independent projects share the same three-file skeleton:

  • CORE.md — fixed principles, mandatory startup sequence, rule-priority hierarchy (Security > Integrity > Quality > Efficiency)
  • AGENT.md — execution behavior, mandatory decision statements, a self-monitoring/deviation-detection table
  • SESSION_INDEX.md — cumulative session memory, versioned and compressed over time, with the original archive preserved

This three-file format isn't new by itself — the AGENTS.md pattern is now an industry standard, common across GitHub. What's different is how these files evolve.

Evidence: failure → rule → cross-domain inheritance

In one project (an e-commerce web app), a concrete incident occurred on 2026-07-20: during session-log compression, 7 open issues and 2 decisions were silently dropped. This got written directly into CORE.md:

"v1.2 — Added the '400-line threshold' rule to §7.1 Step 1... Rationale: unjustified loss of items on 2026-07-20 (7 open issues + 2 decisions)"

The same rule shows up in a fourth project's CORE.md — in a completely different domain (an AI decision system / n8n orchestration layer):

"[Previous project]'s 2026-07-20 violation... this project does not inherit that failure."

This is structurally different from "self-correcting memory" examples that stay within a single repo or framework (e.g., GitHub's pro-workflow, or the AGENTS.md "local norms" pattern): the learning here crosses project and domain boundaries.

Pruned to scale

The format isn't a blind template. The same skeleton produces a ~480-line CORE.md in a large, high-risk project (the trading system), but is deliberately trimmed to 97 lines in a smaller-scale project (the AI decision system) — unnecessary weight (an 8-point security self-check, a code-quality scoring system) isn't carried over. This mirrors the "proportional governance" principle argued in enterprise literature by JFrog: "forcing low-risk, productivity-focused agents through compliance checklists designed for high-stakes systems creates operational paralysis." The difference: JFrog sells this as a platform product; here it's applied through human judgment, at zero added infrastructure cost.

3. Structural evidence the system is "alive" — without exposing project specifics

The three-file skeleton above (CORE/AGENT/SESSION_INDEX) is really just the visible spine of a much larger file family. In one project this family grows to more than 20 files (ARCHITECTURE, ROADMAP, ROLLBACK, PHASE_TRACKER, FAILURE_PATTERNS, TEST_MATRIX, CONFIG_SCHEMA, DEPENDENCIES, and multiple versioned SESSION_INDEX sub-files). Without exposing project-specific content, here are four mechanism types that show this family is a living system, not a static template:

  1. Self-inconsistency detection and flagging. The system notices when one of its own files has gone stale, marks it with the session number the drift was caught in, and states which source should be treated as current. A static documentation file doesn't declare its own invalidity.

  2. Dense cross-referencing. Files aren't isolated; each one references others down to the section number, forming a single knowledge graph. This is structurally different from the isolated, single-file AGENTS.md pattern.

  3. Experience-calibrated rules. The failure-pattern log doesn't contain raw, theoretical rules — it contains thresholds and distinctions distilled from real incidents (false alarms, real outages). A distinction like "when is this a real problem vs. noise" can only be written this precisely after accumulated experience.

  4. Organic file splitting. Memory files show a growth pattern that wasn't planned in advance — they split into sub-versions as need arose over time, not according to a predetermined structure.

Together, these four mechanisms show the protocol is something other than a "human writes, AI reads" model: the files shape the AI's output, and the AI's output (failure logs, inconsistency flags) shapes the files back — a reciprocal, cumulative loop. This loop matters especially because the designer can't read and verify the code line by line — so the system's reliability depends heavily on how sound these self-consistency mechanisms are (the cross-referencing in point 2, the self-inconsistency detection in point 1). The code isn't reviewed line-by-line by a human, but there's a multi-layered cross-check at the protocol level.

4. Consistency of the end-to-end agent structure: same protocol, different agent architectures

The CORE/AGENT/SESSION_INDEX family described so far is the shared "skeleton layer" across all four projects. But this skeleton doesn't impose the same kind of agent structure everywhere — each project defines its own agent architecture inside that skeleton, based on its actual risk surface. This matters because it shows where consistency holds, and where it deliberately doesn't.

What stays fixed (the protocol layer): startup sequence, mandatory decision statements, the self-monitoring/deviation table, the rule-priority hierarchy, the versioning logic of session memory — these are structurally identical across all four projects.

What varies by project (the execution/agent layer):

  • PUSULA has the most explicit multi-agent architecture: Executor and Critic roles are deliberately separated, bound by a rule that they can "never be from the same model family" — meaning the agent that proposes and the agent that reviews are structurally independent. On top of that, there's a separate Policy Engine layer where decisions can only be executed by deterministic code — no AI call is allowed into it. Against prompt injection, it uses a dual-LLM / quarantine pattern: externally sourced text is processed in a context separate from system instructions.
  • NEXUS is single-agent but relies on a layered validation chain: signal generation, backtesting (CPCV/DSR validation), and a shadow/paper-mode observation layer are separate stages that can't override each other — the "agent" is singular, but the decision process is multi-stage, with each stage able to challenge the one before it.
  • Bowlera is built around a single customer-facing execution agent; the distinction here isn't in agent count but in rule type — design/brand-integrity rules (motion preferences, calorie information that can never be hidden) dominate over technical/security rules.
  • Sovereign Engine OS, being an infrastructure layer, organizes its agent architecture more around "authorization routing" — components like githubTokenRouter.ts constrain, at the code level, which operation an agent can perform under which authority.

The real value of seeing this laid out: the protocol layer (how decisions get made, how failures get logged, how work gets handed off) is directly portable across all four projects, while the agent architecture (how many agents, which roles, which separation principles) is redesigned each time based on the project's actual risk surface. What's being carried over isn't a template — it's a decision-making discipline. Agent count and roles are an output of that discipline, not an input to it.

5. The closest examples found on GitHub — and why they're structurally narrower

The closest comparable examples found in a fair search:

Project What it does Difference from this system
rohitg00/pro-workflow Self-correcting memory for Claude Code that learns from corrections, compounding over 50+ sessions (/learn-rule, /wrap-up) Bounded to a single repo/project; no cross-domain inheritance
Eric Ma's AGENTS.md "self-correction" pattern When the agent receives a correction, it logs it as a "local norm" Also single-repo; explicitly scoped as "local," not portable
charleslwang/MI9-Eval Synthetic-scenario runtime governance evaluation Targets framework-level automation, relying on infrastructure rather than a single developer's discipline

The comparison criterion for any new example added to this table stays the same: does the learning cross a single project/repo/framework boundary into a different problem domain, recorded in a file with a date and a rationale? None of the examples found so far do this.

6. Limits — stated plainly

  • This is a case study, not a controlled experiment. How many developers have built something comparable hasn't been measured; the claim should stay at "I haven't found a public example," not "this is proven."
  • Enforcement is behavioral, not technical: there's no physical blocking at the code level, except at critical/high-risk points (e.g., a kill-switch) that are already hard-coded.
  • The system depends on one person's discipline. If a team grows around it, or a handoff is needed, it will likely need the kind of automated/enforced layer that enterprise models provide.
  • The technical correctness of the code isn't verified by the designer reading it line by line — verification relies on the AI's own tests, self-audit output, and (at critical points) the observed behavior of running production systems. The protocol is human-designed and human-overseen at the "decision and discipline layer," but AI-dependent at the "line-level code correctness" layer. This is an important distinction for understanding what the system actually is: a decision-making discipline, not a code-review discipline.

Conclusion

Enterprise agentic AI governance still talks about "adaptive governance" as of 2026 mostly as a goal — the industry's own writing frames it as a needed shift from static to dynamic, not as the current state. The system documented here reaches something like that same goal — governance that learns, evolves, and adapts by domain — not through automation but through discipline, across four real projects, running for months. Whether that makes it a "proven rarity" or "an undocumented practice nobody's written up yet" is something the literature will clarify as it grows.

blocks.html_en: The format isn't a blind template. The same skeleton produces a ~480-line CORE.md in a large, high-risk project (the trading system), but is deliberately trimmed to 97 lines in a smaller-scale project (the AI decision system) — unnecessary weight (an 8-point security self-check, a code-quality scoring system) isn't carried over. blocks.html_en: • PUSULA has the most explicit multi-agent architecture: Executor and Critic roles are deliberately separated, bound by a rule that they can "never be from the same model family" — meaning the agent that proposes and the agent that reviews are structurally independent. On top of that, there's a separate Policy Engine layer where decisions can only be executed by deterministic code — no AI call is allowed into it. Against prompt injection, it uses a dual-LLM / quarantine pattern: externally sourced text is processed in a context separate from system instructions.

content_html_zh:
独立开发者规模的便携式代理治理：四领域案例研究

概括

这是一个基于文件的执行协议，由四个独立的真实生产项目（加密货币交易系统、电子商务网络应用程序、人工智能决策系统和代理基础设施层）手动维护。 构建它的人没有编写一行代码。 他们设计架构、设置规则层次结构并执行纪律；人工智能编写并从技术上执行代码。 这种划分在这里并不是作为警告而提出的，而是系统实际上的样子：不是一个代码项目，而是一个决策和监督协议。 它的质量可以独立于其设计者是否编写代码来判断。

企业 AI 代理治理（MI9、Microsoft Agent 365、JFrog AI Catalog）提供针对规模和自动化进行优化的系统：集中式遥测、策略即代码、运行时执行。 但即使是他们自己的文献也承认两件事：（1）覆盖范围因框架而异，（2）设置和维护成本对于单独或小规模使用来说是不成比例的。

这里描述的协议族（CORE.md / AGENT.md / SESSION_INDEX.md 及其衍生版本）运行在不同的假设上：不是静态模板，而是随着时间的推移自行修改的系统。 一个项目中的具体失败会作为一条过时的、合理的规则写入文件中，并且该规则会被不同领域中完全不同的项目继承。

1. 企业治理自身的局限性

企业对代理人工智能治理的投资正在快速增长——根据 IDC 的数据，组织现在平均将计划人工智能总支出的 16.7% 用于人工智能/代理安全和治理。 但同样的消息来源显示，实施远远落后于意图：

  • 尽管 76% 的受访者拥有首席人工智能官，但只有 13% 的受访者认为他们拥有适当的人工智能治理。
  • 在 235 名大型企业安全领导者中，92% 的人缺乏对其 AI 身份的全面了解； 82% 的人在他们的网络上发现了他们不知道存在的人工智能代理。
  • 由于控制不力，预计到 2027 年，超过 40% 的代理人工智能项目将被取消。

像 MI9 这样的学术/企业运行时治理框架也隐含地承认了同样的事情。 MI9 自己的论文指出：“覆盖范围取决于每个框架的检测功能：支持回调的框架支持全面的行为监控，而 API 包装架构主要公开操作事件。” 换句话说，设计目标与框架无关，但现实世界的覆盖范围却不然。

底线：企业治理在大规模时是必要的，但在中小型企业治理中既沉重又不完整。

2. 另一种模式：单一决策者领导下的生活协议

四个独立项目共享相同的三文件框架：

  • CORE.md — 固定原则、强制启动顺序、规则优先级层次结构（安全 > 完整性 > 质量 > 效率）
  • AGENT.md — 执行行为、强制决策语句、自我监控/偏差检测表
  • SESSION_INDEX.md — 累积会话内存，随着时间的推移进行版本控制和压缩，并保留原始存档

这种三文件格式本身并不新鲜——AGENTS.md 模式现在是一个行业标准，在 GitHub 上很常见。 不同之处在于这些文件的演变方式。

证据：失败→规则→跨域继承

在一个项目（电子商务 Web 应用程序）中，2026 年 7 月 20 日发生了一起具体事件：在会话日志压缩期间，7 个未解决的问题和 2 个决策被悄悄删除。 这被直接写入 CORE.md 中：

“v1.2 — 在 §7.1 第 1 步中添加了“400 行阈值”规则... 理由：2026 年 7 月 20 日发生不合理的物品损失（7 个未决问题 + 2 个决定）”

同样的规则出现在第四个项目的 CORE.md 中 — 在一个完全不同的领域（AI 决策系统/n8n 编排层）：

“[上一个项目] 2026 年 7 月 20 日的违规行为...... 这个项目没有继承这一失败。”

这在结构上与保留在单个存储库或框架内的“自我纠正记忆”示例（例如 GitHub 的支持工作流程或 AGENTS.md“本地规范”模式）不同：这里的学习跨越了项目和领域的边界。

按比例修剪

该格式不是盲目的模板。 同一骨架在大型高风险项目（交易系统）中生成约 480 行 CORE.md，但在较小规模的项目（人工智能决策系统）中被故意修剪为 97 行——不必要的权重（8 点安全自检、代码质量评分系统）不会被保留。 这反映了 JFrog 在企业文献中提出的“比例治理”原则：“强迫低风险、注重生产力的代理通过为高风险系统设计的合规检查表会造成运营瘫痪。” 不同之处：JFrog 将其作为平台产品进行销售；在这里，它是通过人类判断来应用的，基础设施成本增加为零。

3. 系统“活跃”的结构证据——无需暴露项目细节

上面的三文件框架（CORE/AGENT/SESSION_INDEX）实际上只是一个更大文件系列的可见主干。 在一个项目中，这一族文件增长到超过 20 个文件（ARCHITECTURE、ROADMAP、ROLLBACK、PHASE_TRACKER、FAILURE_PATTERNS、TEST_MATRIX、CONFIG_SCHEMA、DEPENDENCIES 和多个版本化的 SESSION_INDEX 子文件）。 在不暴露项目特定内容的情况下，这里有四种机制类型，表明这个系列是一个活的系统，而不是静态模板：

  1. 自不一致检测和标记。 系统会注意到它自己的文件之一何时过时，用捕获偏差的会话号对其进行标记，并指出哪个源应被视为当前源。 静态文档文件不会声明其自身的无效性。
  2. 密集交叉引用。 文件不是孤立的；每个人都引用其他人的部分编号，形成一个知识图。 这在结构上与隔离的单文件 AGENTS.md 模式不同。
  3. 经验校准的规则。 故障模式日志不包含原始的理论规则——它包含从真实事件（误报、真实中断）中提取的阈值和区别。 像“什么时候这是一个真正的问题与噪音”之类的区别只能在积累经验后才能精确地写出来。
  4. 有机文件分割。 内存文件显示出一种未提前计划的增长模式——它们随着时间的推移根据需要分裂成子版本，而不是根据预定的结构。

这四种机制共同表明，该协议不是“人类写入，人工智能读取”模型：文件塑造人工智能的输出，人工智能的输出（失败日志、不一致标志）塑造文件——一个相互的、累积的循环。 这个循环尤其重要，因为设计人员无法逐行读取和验证代码，因此系统的可靠性在很大程度上取决于这些自洽机制的健全程度（第 2 点中的交叉引用，第 1 点中的自不一致检测）。 代码不是由人工逐行审查，但在协议级别有多层交叉检查。

4. 端到端代理结构的一致性：相同协议，不同代理架构

到目前为止描述的 CORE/AGENT/SESSION_INDEX 系列是所有四个项目共享的“骨架层”。 但这个骨架并没有在所有地方都采用相同类型的代理结构——每个项目都根据其实际风险面在该骨架内定义自己的代理架构。 这很重要，因为它显示了一致性在哪里成立，在哪里故意不成立。

保持固定的内容（协议层）：启动顺序、强制决策语句、自我监控/偏差表、规则优先级层次结构、会话内存的版本控制逻辑——这些在所有四个项目中在结构上都是相同的。

因项目而异（执行/代理层）：

  • PUSULA 拥有最明确的多智能体架构：执行者和评论家角色被故意分开，受到“永远不能来自同一个模型系列”的规则的约束——这意味着提出建议的智能体和审查的智能体在结构上是独立的。 最重要的是，有一个单独的策略引擎层，其中的决策只能由确定性代码执行——不允许人工智能调用。 针对提示注入，它使用双 LLM/隔离模式：外部来源的文本在与系统指令分开的上下文中进行处理。
  • NEXUS 是单代理，但依赖于分层验证链：信号生成、回溯测试（CPCV/DSR 验证）和影子/纸张模式观察层是独立的阶段，不能相互覆盖——“代理”是单一的，但决策过程是多阶段的，每个阶段都能够挑战之前的阶段。
  • Bowlera 是围绕一个面向客户的执行代理构建的；这里的区别不在于代理数量，而在于规则类型——设计/品牌完整性规则（运动偏好、永远无法隐藏的卡路里信息）主导技术/安全规则。
  • Sovereign Engine OS 作为基础设施层，更多地围绕“授权路由”组织其代理架构——像 githubTokenRouter.ts 这样的组件在代码级别限制代理可以在哪个权限下执行哪些操作。

看到这一布局的真正价值是：协议层（如何做出决策、如何记录故障、如何移交工作）可以直接在所有四个项目之间移植，而代理架构（有多少代理、哪些角色、哪些分离原则）每次都会根据项目的实际风险面进行重新设计。 被继承的不是模板，而是决策规则。 代理数量和角色是该学科的输出，而不是输入。

6. 限制——明确说明

  • 这是一个案例研究，而不是对照实验。 有多少开发者开发了类似的东西还没有被测量过；主张应该停留在“我还没有找到公开的例子”，而不是“这已被证明”。
  • 执行是行为性的，而不是技术性的：除了已经硬编码的关键/高风险点（例如终止开关）之外，代码级别没有物理阻塞。
  • 该系统取决于一个人的纪律。 如果团队围绕它成长，或者需要交接，它可能需要企业模型提供的那种自动化/强制层。
  • 代码的技术正确性并不是由设计者逐行阅读来验证的——验证依赖于人工智能自己的测试、自我审核输出以及（在关键点）运行生产系统的观察到的行为。 该协议在“决策和纪律层”是人工设计和人工监督的，但在“行级代码正确性”层依赖于人工智能。 这是理解系统实际是什么的一个重要区别：决策规则，而不是代码审查规则。

结论

截至 2026 年，企业代理人工智能治理仍然将“自适应治理”视为一个目标——行业自己的写作将其描述为从静态到动态的必要转变，而不是当前状态。 这里记录的系统达到了类似的目标——按领域学习、发展和适应的治理——不是通过自动化，而是通过纪律，跨越四个真实项目，运行数月。 这是否使其成为“已被证明的稀有”或“尚未被记录下来的实践”，随着文献的发展，将会澄清这一点。
